Thanks Marissa — this is great, appreciate the clear recap. A few clarifying points from our side before the deep-dive: 

1) Auth: We prefer OIDC (our SSO is Okta) and would like short-lived tokens that are rotated server-side. We want guidance on whether to mint Redwood tokens from our backend or use a client-side flow for embedded experiences.

2) Context size / tokens: Typical session context for our use case is ~2k tokens (user + retrieved docs). For longer responses we’d like a sensible default for max_tokens that protects latency. Any guidance for a 2k input context?

3) Stop sequences + streaming: If we stream partial tokens back to the client, what is Redwood’s behavior for stop sequences? Will the server send an explicit termination event, or do we need to detect token-level signals?

4) Embeddings / reranking: Are there recommended embedding dims/models for semantic reranking vs simple vector search? Also curious about options for approximate vs exact indexes (FAISS HNSW vs disk-backed solutions).

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@acme.com>
Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>, Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-03-26T08:15:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Integration follow-up: SDK auth, routing, and request/response schema questions

Alex — great questions. Below are concise recommendations and the behavioral notes we discussed. I’ve kept this focused so your eng team can digest before the call.

1) Auth / SDK patterns
- Recommended: Server-side OIDC integration (Okta) + short-lived Redwood session tokens. Flow: 
  * Your backend authenticates the user via Okta and mints a short-lived (1–5 minute) signed JWT.
  * Backend exchanges the signed JWT with Redwood auth endpoint to receive a scoped session token (scoped to the user/route).
  * Client calls to Redwood use the session token; long-lived credentials remain on your side.
- Rationale: avoids embedding long-lived API keys in clients, supports audit/KMS controls, and lets you enforce per-user routing/policy.
- See SDK auth guide: https://redwood.app/docs/sdk/auth (attached sample shows exchange flow).

2) Routing & deployment
- Suggested routing: primary -> Dedicated (us-east) for predictable latency; fallback -> Redwood hosted region (us-west) when capacity constrained.
- Policy knobs: route by model latency profile, cost tier, or region. We can preconfigure per-customer policies for canary/rollout.

3) Structured output & tool calling
- If you need deterministic JSON structures and type guarantees, function-calling (signature-backed) is best. The SDK has helpers to validate returned fields and retry on partial/malformed outputs.
- If you prefer schema-first but outside function-calling, use strict JSON-schema validation on the response and reject/repair outputs via a small post-processing step.

4) Embeddings & rerankers
- Model recs: start with a semi-compact embedding (2048-d float16 or 1536 for lower-cost) depending on recall vs cost.
- Index recs: HNSW (FAISS) or Annoy for low-latency approximate nearest neighbor; for exact disk-backed lookups consider IVF/PQ with periodic rebuilds.
- Reranking flow: retrieve top-K (~100) by vector distance then run a lightweight cross-encoder or relevance scorer to rerank top candidates. This reduces latency while improving precision.

5) Request/response schema: chat vs completions, tokenization, max_tokens, stop, streaming
- Chat vs completions: Use chat endpoints for multi-turn flows where role separation (system/user/assistant) and message deltas matter. Use completions for single-turn generation where you send a prompt and expect a single output. Chat endpoints have built-in state handling semantics and are typically preferred for assistants.
- Tokenization: token counts are model-dependent; the SDK exposes a tokenizer util to estimate tokens pre-flight. For a 2k-token input, measure with the target model’s tokenizer (we can run a quick tokenization pass on your sample documents in the deep-dive).
- max_tokens guidance: for a 2k input context, start with max_tokens=256 for responses to balance latency and utility. If you need longer responses, consider streaming with incremental rendering and conservative max_tokens per request (256–512) plus follow-up generation if needed.
- Stop sequences: stop tokens are honored by the server on both completions and chat endpoints. In streaming mode, the server will stop emitting tokens once the stop condition is met and emit a final completion/"done" event. We provide a clear [DONE] sentinel event in the stream and a final message chunk with metadata (length, truncated true/false).
- Streaming semantics: the SDK stream yields partial text deltas and structured events (token, role, function_call chunk, and a final done event). Your client can render partial content as it arrives; implement idempotent handlers because the SDK may emit correction tokens (rare) and a finalization event that confirms the full output.

Attachments: sample SDK code demonstrates function-calling + streaming patterns and a small tokenization helper (see redwood-sdk-sample-code.zip). The architecture sketch includes a recommended flow for a retrieval + rerank pipeline (acme-mvp-architecture.pdf).

Next steps: I’ll join the 3/26 11am PT deep-dive and we’ll do a short live demo of function-calling + streaming + a rerank example. Dev will show the SDK snippet live.

If it helps, we can also run a quick tokenization pass on a few representative sessions before the call — please drop a small sample document into the shared folder or send it to me.

Cheers,
Marissa
